title: Gloop & Messy Play
strapline: Cornflour that can't decide if it's solid or liquid — and all the gloriously messy trays in between.
intent: Meet materials that break the rules: cornflour gloop is hard when you squeeze it and runs through your fingers the moment you let go — a genuine scientific puzzle in a tray.
Build sensory confidence at each child's own pace — some dive in to the elbows, some start with one fingertip or a spoon, and both are progress.
Grow a vocabulary of texture and change: slimy, drippy, stretchy, crumbly, cold, oozing — words earned through the fingertips.
Strengthen hands, wrists and fingers through squeezing, scooping, swirling and dragging in resistant, unpredictable materials.
Make marks and early meaning in trays — trails, swirls, letters, roads — where every surface wipes clean for another go.
Mix, combine and transform on purpose: adding colour, adding water, watching two things become one new thing.
implementation: Mix the gloop with the children watching — powder, then water, then the moment it turns — so the transformation is the first provocation.
Model the gloop paradox playfully: punch it (solid), then open your hand and let it pour (liquid), and wonder aloud why.
Never force hands in: offer spoons, sticks and tools as a bridge for cautious children, sit close, and let watching count as joining in.
Give the describing words at the exact moment of sensation — 'ooh, it's oozing off my fingers' beats any word card.
Rotate the trays across weeks — gloop, cooked spaghetti, jelly, oats, foam soap — so texture-talk keeps growing rather than repeating.
Add a drop of colour to one corner and let children do the mixing — marbling is theirs to discover, not yours to demonstrate.
Use messy trays for purposeful marks with older children: name letters in the foam, roads through the oats, but keep it invitation not task.
key_questions: Is it a solid or a liquid — how could we find out?
What happens when you squeeze it really hard, then stop?
What does it feel like — can you find a word for it?
What do you think will happen if we add the blue?
Can you make a mark that stays? Why does it disappear?
Which tray was your favourite this week — what was different about it?

impact.text: Children plunge into the trays with enthusiasm and their own agenda — swirling, squeezing, letting gloop ooze between their fingers.
Children discover that gloop behaves as solid under pressure and liquid at rest, and test the switch again and again.
Children ask why the gloop goes hard, why the jelly wobbles, why the foam disappears — and expect proper answers.
Children name what they're touching and ask about what's new in the tray — 'what's that?' — building words from sensation.
Children try out freshly-heard texture words — oozing, slimy, stretchy — in their own commentary.
Children drag trails and swirls through the trays, and begin to say what their marks are after making them.
Children mix colours and materials deliberately to see what happens, choosing what goes in next.
Cautious children edge in — first watching, then a spoon, then a fingertip — growing in confidence to try something new.

enhancements: Two-tray contrast: gloop beside dry cornflour powder, so children feel before-and-after in the same session.
Pipettes and small pots of coloured water for slow, controlled marbling into white gloop.
Cooked spaghetti with tongs, scissors and bowls — slippery cutting practice with instant portions.
Frozen jelly with small-world figures set inside — melt, dig and rescue.
Combs, forks, rollers and pattern scrapers for repeat-pattern mark-making in foam or gloop.
A mirror under a clear tray base, so children see the underside of their swirls appear as they drag.
Warm and cold versions of the same tray side by side — temperature as its own texture.

playing_exploring: Messy trays are pure open-ended finding-out — no product, no right answer, just what the material does next.
Children choose their own way in — hands, tools or watchful waiting — and the tray meets them there.
active_learning: Children repeat the squeeze-release cycle dozens of times, refining their theory of what the gloop will do.
For cautious children, getting both hands in at all is a hard-won achievement worth celebrating.
creating_thinking: Gloop gives children a genuine anomaly to reason about — it fits neither 'solid' nor 'liquid' and they know it.
They carry ideas between trays — 'it's like the jelly but colder' — comparing, linking and predicting.
